title: Heads-up
summary: One on one: very wide ranges, constant aggression and a pair worth more than at a full table.

idea.text: In heads-up the button is also the small blind: it acts first before the flop and last after it. You pay a blind every hand, so waiting for a good hand doesn't work: ranges are very wide, and aggression decides.

ranges.text:
Reference points at 100 BB:
- The **button** opens **70–85%** of hands to 2–2.5 BB. Only the weakest offsuit hands like 72o and 83o fold.
- The **big blind** defends about **60–70%** against a 2–2.5 BB open and 3-bets many strong hands and some bluffs.
- Any ace, any pair and two broadway cards are strong heads-up hands.

postflop.text:
After the flop:
- Pairs are rare, so **high card and one pair** win often; don't fold them too easily.
- Big blind check-raises and button **floats** are routine.
- You play many hands against the same opponent: notice how often he folds and adjust (the Exploit lesson).

Heads-up against the PokerALL bots is the best practice for this: in a series every hand counts.

q-q4.q: Heads-up, 100 BB, you are on the button with Q4o. What is usually best?
q-q4.explain: Q4o is well inside a 70–85% heads-up opening range.

t1.q: Who acts first before the flop in heads-up?
t1.explain: Preflop the button acts first; after the flop it acts last.

t2.q: About how much of the deck does the button open heads-up?
t2.explain: Only the weakest offsuit hands fold.

t3.q: Why is one pair worth more heads-up than at a full table?
options: It is easier to bluff with
There is one opponent, and he rarely has a pair
t3.explain: With one opponent the chance that he has better is much lower.
